opus-5.5.text:
I think culture is a tool, not a decoration. A lot of people talk about culture as if it's something you put on the wall: "we value innovation," "we value openness." But in my view, culture should exist to help the company achieve its mission. If it doesn't do that, it's just a slogan.

When we started building the company around Taichi, I asked: what kind of behavior do we actually need for this business to succeed? We're building developer infrastructure, a programming language and compiler stack. That means we need people who care deeply about technical quality, who can think long-term, and who are honest about what's working and what isn't. So the culture should reward those things. If someone finds a bug in a core design, even one they wrote, we want them to say it out loud immediately instead of hiding it. That's not because honesty sounds nice. It's because in infrastructure, hidden problems compound and become very expensive later.

Second, culture should help people make decisions when you're not in the room. As the company grows, a founder can't approve everything. Culture is what lets an engineer facing a trade-off, say speed versus correctness, or a quick fix versus a proper solution, make roughly the same call the leadership would. A good culture is basically a compressed decision-making algorithm shared by everyone.

Third, I think culture has to evolve with the business. What works for five people in a small room doesn't automatically work for fifty or five hundred. Early on, you want a lot of flexibility and ownership, everyone doing a bit of everything. Later, you might need more process, more clarity about responsibilities. Some founders get very attached to the early culture and treat any change as betrayal. I don't think that's right. The goal is the mission, and culture should serve it.

And finally, you can't fake it. People watch what you do, not what you say. If you say you value long-term thinking but you reward whoever ships the flashiest demo this week, then your real culture is short-termism. So for me, the most important part of building culture is consistency between what the leaders say and how they actually make decisions, who they hire, who they promote, and what they celebrate.

r001.rationale: The response says culture should help the company achieve its mission and calls it a slogan if it does not.

r002.rationale: It recommends culture based on behaviors the business needs, but does not say to build it around common ground identified with by a small group.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think culture is often misunderstood as a nice-to-have, something you put on a poster. For me, culture is really the operating system of the company. It's the set of defaults people fall back on when there's no rule written down and nobody senior is in the room. And that's most of the time, honestly. You can't write a process for every situation, so culture is what fills in the gaps.

At Taichi, when we started, we were a small team coming out of research, and a lot of our early culture came from that background. In research you have to be honest about what doesn't work. You can't fake a benchmark. So one thing I cared about a lot was this idea of intellectual honesty: if something is slow, say it's slow. If a design is wrong, say it before we ship it, not after. That sounds obvious, but it's actually hard to maintain once a company has customers and deadlines and people are afraid of looking bad.

So how should culture serve the business? I'd say in three ways. First, it should make decisions faster. If everyone shares the same priorities, you don't need a meeting for every small thing. Second, it should attract the right people and, maybe more importantly, repel the wrong ones. When we hired, I'd rather lose a strong candidate who didn't fit than bring in someone who'd quietly erode how the team works. And third, culture should let the company survive mistakes. Every startup makes big mistakes. The question is whether people feel safe enough to surface them early.

One thing I'd caution against is building culture that serves the founder's ego instead of the business. It's easy to say "we value X" because you personally like X. But culture has to be tested against reality: does this actually help us build better software, serve users better, move faster? If not, it's just decoration. And I'd also say culture shouldn't be frozen. What worked for ten people doesn't automatically work for fifty, so you have to be willing to revisit it honestly, the same way you'd revisit a technical design.

r001.rationale: The candidate says culture should be tested against whether it helps build better software, serve users, or move faster, and that culture without such benefit is decoration. This gives business contribution as the test for keeping it.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions that early culture came from a small research team, but does not recommend building culture around common ground that a small group identifies with.

astra-6.text:
I think company culture should help people make decisions that serve the business. It should be practical. When two priorities conflict, or someone faces a situation we haven’t discussed before, the culture should give them a useful way to think about what to do.

For example, if we say we care about customers, that should affect which problems we work on and how quickly we respond when something goes wrong. If we say we value innovation, we need to give people room to experiment and accept that some experiments will fail.

And the founders have to demonstrate those values through their own decisions. People pay attention to what you reward and what you tolerate. Ultimately, a good culture helps a team work together and make better decisions without needing approval for every small thing.

r001.rationale: It says culture should help people make business-serving decisions, but does not say to retain a culture based on its contribution to business success.

r002.rationale: It discusses shared values and founders demonstrating them, but does not recommend building culture around common ground identified by a small group.

sol-6.1.text:
I think company culture should help people make decisions that serve the business. It should give the team a shared understanding of what matters, how we work together, and how we handle tradeoffs, especially when there isn’t a clear rule or someone there to tell you what to do.

If we say we value innovation, for example, people need room to experiment and learn from failures. If we say customers come first, that needs to show up in how we prioritize work. Culture becomes useful when it shapes everyday behavior, rather than just being words on a wall.

r001.rationale: The response says culture should guide decisions that serve the business, but does not make business contribution the test for whether to retain a culture.

r002.rationale: It mentions a shared understanding, but does not recommend building culture around common ground identified by a small group.
